note_tweet.text:
Most security scanning today works the noisy way.
A tool reads your code, matches patterns, and gives you a long list of warnings. Then a human has to check each one to see if it is real.

There is a faster way: let an AI agent do the security review. It reads the code like an engineer would, and looks for real vulnerabilities (bugs an attacker can use).

But there is a catch. A finding is only a guess until someone proves it. And after that, someone still has to write the fix and check that the fix works.

OpenAI has open-sourced Codex Security, a CLI and TypeScript SDK that tries to cover this whole path.

The idea is simple: find, validate, fix.

1/. Install it and sign in: npm install --global @openai/codex-security, then cs login.
2/. Run cs scan . in your repo.
3/. It validates the candidate findings and generates patches.
4/. You get a Markdown report, and you can export the results.

The tool does the checking work, so you look at fewer, better findings.

How it works:

Scan scope: 
you can scan the full repo, selected paths, or only Git changes (cs scan . --diff origin/main).

Deep mode: 
it repeats the Standard scan several times and removes 

duplicate findings.
Threat model: each scan saves a threat model (a description of what can be attacked and how) with the results. cs policy . drafts or updates your SECURITY.md.

Triage: it can find duplicates, rate severity against your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.

What you get:
• Exports to SARIF, JSON and CSV
• Tracking in Linear, Jira or GitHub
• A GitHub Action for scheduled scans (the example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan)
• Works with OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI and Cheaper Inference
• Apache-2.0 license, ~13k GitHub stars
One thing to know: it needs an API key or login, and the README says some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require Trusted Access for Cyber.

What I find interesting is the diff scan is the useful part. You can run it on every pull request, so the agent reviews only what changed and not the whole repo each time.

Links 
https://t.co/Q3hKqlbsqp

Product designer Tony Gorb shipped 83 releases of an open-source app in 64 days with Claude Code, Codex and Cursor running in parallel. The agents wrote the code. He kept every merge and every release.

🔥 From the first commit on August 4 to v0.22.0 on October 7, GitHub shows those 83 version tags and 303 merged pull requests. 220 were the work; the other 83 were the release PR each version opens.

The point wasn't a new tool. He wrote one contract, AGENTS.md, that every agent reads first: reuse an existing named pattern unless he asked for a brainstorm, and treat a session as iterate (no build, no unit tests, no end-to-end) or as checkpoint (buy confidence once).

From September 7, each task gets its own git worktree, with its own ports and its own copy of the library, so the three agents can work at the same time without editing each other's files. A wrapper creates the worktree, so isolation doesn't depend on an agent remembering an env var.

A sloppy rule almost burned him. A line that said never commit, push, stash, reset or checkout his tree was read as forbidding the branch itself, and a whole fix landed on main on August 29. The rewrite is blunt: nothing merges or ships on an agent's own initiative.

One night, while he was asleep, a Claude session ran ten more sessions across four worktrees to QA the 0.18.0 release. It found 85 issues and no blocker. One security session never finished its dynamic tests, because the auto-mode safety classifier blocked them.

Today the repo is still early: 4 GitHub stars, latest tag v0.22.2 on November 2. Copy the written contract and the human gate, not the release count.

🔗 Link in the first reply 👇

NVIDIA SkillEvaluator is on GitHub Trending today. The useful engineering question is whether a skill improves the task outcome. A clean static report is an earlier checkpoint, and treating it as the final answer can hide the failure you actually care about.

For a first rehearsal, use a disposable directory with Git and uv installed. Clone the official example:
git clone --depth 1 https://t.co/VcN262hEuf
cd SkillEvaluator
Then run:
uv run --python 3.13 skillevaluator quality-check src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer -r cli -r json -o reports/first-quality

The documented path needs no API key, GPU, scanner or Docker. Inspect both the terminal findings and reports/first-quality/skillevaluator-quality.json. A completed passing quality check should exit 0. If setup fails, resolve the dependency error before interpreting missing output as a low score. Record the checkout commit with git rev-parse HEAD so another run has a meaningful reference.

The important limit: this command checks static quality. Publication evidence remains INCOMPLETE; security coverage and live agent impact require separate evaluation. Do not generalize its result into “safe” or “makes coding better.”

My next acceptance test would use a small set of independently checked tasks, hold the model and permissions constant, and compare runs with and without the skill. Count wrong outputs and unexpected actions alongside completion time. That is a proposed evaluation method, not a benchmark result from this rehearsal. A trending repository earns an investigation; your own failure cases decide whether it belongs in the workflow.

Reference: https://t.co/NVZhKmyQXC

if your ADE doesn't do this, you ngmi, prateek wrote, screenshotting a setup running more than one coding agent on the same task at once. Theo, who built T3 Code, replied that his hasn't looked different since 2025. Worth sitting with that exchange for a second.

T3 Code is free, MIT licensed, 27,600 GitHub stars as of mid October, and drives Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, and Google Antigravity from one app. Good software. But each thread still runs one agent at a time on one branch. Orca, the other big entrant in this category, got to 79,000 stars doing something closer to what prateek is asking for: git worktree isolation per task and a race mode that runs the same prompt through several agents and keeps the best result. Superset is positioning itself as a control plane above both. None of them, per the people actually using them, fully solve running agents together on one task rather than one after another.

That's the gap Campfire was built to close. Run Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, and OpenHands side by side in a single browser tab, each in its own git worktree so nothing collides. Race the same task across every backend you have installed and compare results directly, the way Orca does, except across five tools instead of one vendor's lineup. Permission voting handles the part nobody mentions in these threads: when multiple agents want to touch the same repo, majority rules approves, any single deny blocks, and a 30 second timer keeps it from stalling. A Kanban board builds itself from the agents' own tool calls, and a cost dashboard shows what each backend burned.

Running agents one at a time was never the ceiling on this stuff. Coordinating them was always the real work, and most of the category still skips it.

note_tweet.text:
Google Chrome raised Codex's web-development check pass rate from 54% to 82% in its own evaluation, just by adding a skill.

No model retraining required.

Claude Code improved from 57% to 88%, while Antigravity went from 58% to 94%.

The project is called Modern Web Guidance, an open-source collection of skills developed with contributions from the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams.

The problem is that AI coding agents often generate outdated JavaScript and CSS patterns for functionality that modern browsers already support natively.

Instead of building custom implementations, agents can use:

→ Popover API: Create native popovers without manually implementing every interaction.

→ CSS Anchor Positioning: Position tooltips and menus relative to their triggers.

→ Container Queries: Build responsive components based on their container dimensions.

→ View Transitions: Animate interface changes using browser-native APIs.

The repository contains 203 expert-reviewed guides covering 250 web platform features, including performance, accessibility, security, and browser compatibility.

Under the hood, its CLI combines local semantic search with BM25 to retrieve relevant guidance directly into an agent's context.

It also includes a scanner that identifies supported legacy patterns in existing codebases and suggests modern alternatives.

The team evaluated agents with and without the skills using Playwright-based checks.

The reported improvements are automated check pass rates on specific web-development tasks, not general coding success rates. Codex and Claude Code were evaluated on 215 tasks, while Antigravity used 214.

The repository has crossed 18,000 GitHub stars.

Before asking for a more capable coding model, make sure the one you already have knows what modern browsers can do.

Open source. Software licensed under Apache 2.0, with guide content under CC BY 4.0.

GitHub: https://t.co/SMYVxC5lhi

article.plain_text:
How I use Grok Bot as a super admin over my Macs, my phone and my agents, and why the button that matters most says Allow
The short version, if you're saving this for later:
The setup. One chat app on my phone and my desk reaches a cloud computer, three Macs, my iPhone and nine connected accounts. I call it my super admin layer.
The rule. Wide reach, narrow permission. Anything that sends, posts, buys, deletes or runs a command on one of my Macs stops as a card I have to answer.
What runs alone. Routines: a morning recap, a watcher every 15 minutes, a release radar, an evening report. They prepare. They don't publish.
Four things to copy. A device map, a set of Ask first rules, a routine template, and a "never delegate" list.
The honest part. I can't prove yet that it gives me back more hours than it costs me in reading and tapping. That's the test I'm starting this week.
 
A super admin should reach everything and do almost nothing alone
This week I wrote a sentence to my own bots that turned out to be the whole design: the heavy work always stays on the Macs, and Grok Bot is my super admin that sends missions to the machines.
Before that, when I was trying to explain it to myself in French, I called it a shadow super admin. A kind of external god mode. Everything real runs somewhere else, on machines I own, and this one layer sits above it, sees all of it, and can reach any of it from the phone in my pocket.
"God mode" sounds like power. In practice the opposite is what makes it work. The layer that can reach everything is the layer that's allowed to do the least on its own. It reads, it prepares, it dispatches, it drafts. When something would leave the system or change it for real, it stops and asks me.
That's the claim of this piece. A personal super admin isn't valuable because it can touch every device. It's valuable if the time it gives back is bigger than the time I spend supervising it. I call that difference Net Autonomy: the hours AI gives back, minus the supervision tax.
Reach is cheap. Permission is the product.
This article is the human side of the setup. The machine side, with the three layers, the usage audit and what broke, is in my previous piece, "Decide Up, Work Down." Here I want to show what it looks like from where I actually sit: one chat, a phone, a few rules, and a lot of things I've decided never to hand over.
Everything I own is one sentence away
Here's the map. Names of projects, accounts and machines stay out on purpose. The capabilities are real and documented, and I've linked the docs at the end.
The core fact about Grok Bot is simple: it's an agent with its own persistent computer in the cloud, with a browser, a terminal and files. The FAQ says it plainly: "Closing the app, laptop, or phone does not stop a background turn or routine." Everything else in my setup hangs off that.
On top of the cloud computer, I've registered my own devices. Right now that's three Macs, two of which are Mac Studios that do the heavy work, and my iPhone. Then come the connectors: two Gmail accounts, two Google Calendars, GitHub, Vercel, Stripe, a database backend, and X.
 
A few details from the docs matter more than they look.
The phone is not always reachable. The mobile docs say "The Bot can reach your phone only while Grok Bot is open on it." So my iPhone is a device I can talk from at any time, and a device the bots can act on only when I've opened the app. I like that limit. It means the phone is mine first.
The Macs ask by default. In Settings, each registered computer has a setting called Execution on this computer, with three choices: Ask every time, Always allow, Never allow. The docs set the default to Ask every time and recommend Never allow "unless a Bot has a specific reason to work on your local files." That's the right instinct. Most of what I want from the Macs comes back as a summary from the machine itself, not as a bot typing commands into it.
And voice is a real input. On an iPhone with an Action Button you can map it to "Start Voice Chat" with a Bot. I dictated the request for this very article in French, hesitations included, and the article you're reading is in English. That's what "one sentence away" means in practice: the distance between a thought and a mission is one message, in whatever language I happen to be thinking in.
 
Reach is cheap, permission is the product
Anyone can wire an agent to a lot of accounts. The work is deciding what it may do without you.
Grok Bot handles this with a layer called Auto Review. Before the bot runs a command, uses a connected app or uses its computer, the action is checked. Most actions just run. When one needs me, an approval card shows up in the chat with the operation and its inputs. I get Allow once, Always allow, or Deny. Always allow saves a rule so similar actions run on their own next time.
The docs are honest about the limits of that, and I'd put this sentence on the wall of anyone building agents: "An approval controls the proposed action. It does not reverse work already completed." And this one: "Auto Review is model-based and should complement, not replace, least privilege and explicit approval boundaries."
So I don't rely on the reviewer alone. I write my boundaries down. You can add up to 20 "Ask first" rules and up to 20 "Allow automatically" rules, each up to 1,000 characters. If both kinds match an action, Ask first wins. Here's the shape of mine, generalized so you can paste it.
 
Two rules in there carry most of the weight. The X rule exists because a public post is the most irreversible thing my system can do in a normal day. Every post is a card first, and the card can only go out after a later message from me that names it. This morning one tweet went out that way, and its source link went out the same way a bit later, as a separate tap.
The money rule is there because the docs are clear that a card saved in the bot's vault "fills in at checkout without a separate approval each time." If you want to approve every payment, the advice is simple: don't save the card. I'd rather tap.
The phone isn't the remote control. The approval is.
There's a timing detail I didn't know until I read it. When work starts from a chat message, the card waits for my answer and doesn't expire. When a routine or another bot raises the card, it expires after about 30 minutes. That's a good default for someone who doesn't want to live on call. If I'm training, eating or listening to a record, the background ask simply lapses and gets raised again later. Nothing happens while I'm not looking.
 
Routines are the part that works while I'm not there
A chat is something I start. A routine is something the system starts on its own clock. This is where a super admin earns its keep or quietly burns your week.
The routines docs define two triggers: a schedule, or an event such as a GitHub notification, an email to the bot's own address, a Slack message or a webhook call. Routines run in the cloud while the laptop is closed. A bot can own up to 50 of them, schedules have to be at least five minutes apart, and all your routines together can run up to 300 times an hour.
Here are the ones my news and growth bot runs today. All in Madrid time.
 
Look at the last column. Every routine I run prepares. None of them publishes, sends or buys. The docs say the same thing in four words, and it's the best routine advice I've read: "Automate preparation before execution."
The watcher is the one I'm most curious about. I wanted my X likes and my GitHub stars to become work without me asking, and now they do: I like a post on my phone, and within about 15 minutes there's a draft waiting, with a source. The small honest problem is cost. Every run spends usage. In my last audit, one monitoring routine that ran every 30 minutes, about 336 times a week, cost 4% of my weekly usage by itself. The watcher runs twice as often, 96 times a day. If each run cost the same, it would be around 8% of my week. I haven't measured it yet, and the docs warn that "an hourly schedule, a short interval, or a Slack trigger on a busy channel can use a week of usage in a day." It's on the list.
Here's the template I use for any new routine. It's mostly the docs' own checklist, with two lines I added after things went wrong.
 
The two lines I added are the last two before review. "If nothing new, stay silent" comes from the companion article: my supervising bots were reading and reporting things nobody needed. The foundation dossier I wrote this year has a sentence for it: "The best interface may sometimes be one that stays silent." The cost line comes from that 4% routine.
 
Many bots, one rulebook, one shared computer
I don't run one assistant. I run a small roster, and each bot has one job.
 
The roster is designed around a cost I found the hard way. In the companion piece I describe the audit: 87% of my usage came from the three bots supervising the machines, because they were reading logs and debugging things themselves. The fix was a rule: bots only decide and dispatch, and diagnosis, retries and monitoring run on the Macs, which send back short summaries. That rule is now written once in shared memory, and every bot sees it.
Shared memory is the quiet feature that makes a roster feel like one system. Each bot keeps its own conversations and role, but a few facts about me are shared by all of them, and the rules I record as shared travel with them. The "heavy work stays on the Macs" rule went in once, and I didn't have to repeat it bot by bot. The same goes for the skills library: a method saved once as a skill can be used by any bot that has the access it needs.
Then there's the part of the design I want everyone to read twice. All bots on an account share one cloud computer. The docs say it in one line: "Do not use separate Bots as a security boundary." Files, browser sessions and command-line credentials on that computer are available to every bot. Deleting a bot "does not remove shared-computer files or browser sessions."
So my roster is a way to divide attention and cost, not a way to divide trust. If one bot can reach a login, assume all of them can. That's exactly why the approval rules matter more than the roster.
What it changes in an ordinary day
The Altreality idea I keep testing is simple: machines should absorb friction so the world becomes available again. So here's the honest version of what this setup changes in a normal day, without dressing it up.
The day starts with something already done. The recap lands at 8:30 with the news worth my attention, the releases that matter, the posts worth answering, and a plan for the day's four posting slots. I don't open twenty tabs to build that picture. I read one screen.
What I liked yesterday has already become work. A post I liked on my phone is a draft tweet with its source. A repo I starred is a short note on what it does and whether it's worth a post. I didn't write a ticket for either.
My decisions are mostly taps. A draft arrives, I read it, I say go or I say no. A command on a Mac shows up as a card with the exact command. I can answer from the phone. I don't need to be at a desk, and that's the real change. The desk stops being the only place where the work can move forward.
The heavy work happens where it should. The Mac Studios run their missions and report in a few lines. If nothing changed, I hear nothing. Silence is the report.
There are also things I can do that I don't want to oversell. I could start a voice chat from the Action Button while walking. I could ask the bot to move a calendar event or add a reminder from wherever I am. Those capabilities exist and I've connected the phone. Whether they return real time, or just make it easier to stay on call, is precisely what I don't know yet.
That last sentence is the one that matters. The foundation dossier names the trap better than I can: "One may build agents to save time and then spend every evening managing them." A super admin in your pocket can become a manager in your pocket. The same phone that lets me approve a post from a walk can turn the walk into a meeting.
My rule for that is boring and it works for me so far: the system can wait. Background approvals expire. Routines prepare and hold. Nothing important is designed to need me within minutes. If it ever is, that's a design bug, not a reason to check the phone more often.
What I never delegate
This is the list I'd keep even if every agent became perfect tomorrow. Copy it and cross out what doesn't fit your life.
 
Two notes on the list.
Sign-ins are the one place where the product already behaves the way I'd want. Bots sign in from a vault without seeing the passwords, and for steps like single sign-on, a passkey or a CAPTCHA, the bot hands me control of its computer. I do the step, press I'm done, and it continues. The docs' rule is also mine: no password, code or API key goes into an ordinary chat.
The last block is the one people skip. Deciding when a system is allowed to interrupt you is a delegation decision, and it's the one that shapes your day the most. Notifications can be switched off bot by bot, and that's where I'd start. If every bot can ping you, you haven't built a super admin. You've hired five interns who all have your number.
The strongest objection: one chat that can reach everything can break everything
Here's the case against my setup, as fairly as I can put it.
One account, one cloud computer, every login on it, every bot able to use it. If something goes wrong in that layer, from a bad instruction to a page the bot reads with hidden instructions in it, the blast radius is my whole digital life. Simon Willison has a name for the dangerous combination: the lethal trifecta, an agent with access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out. A super admin has all three by design.
Second, approvals have a cost of their own. Every card is a few seconds of my attention, and attention spent on cards is supervision tax. Too many cards and I start approving without reading, which is worse than no cards at all.
Third, the reviewer is a model. The docs say so themselves. Model-based review is a seatbelt, not a guarantee.
I don't think any of this is fatal, but I don't have a clean answer either. What I can say is what I do about each one.
On blast radius, I keep the outward channels behind Ask first rules: email, posts, messages, money, production. Reading is wide. Sending is narrow. That's the only part of the trifecta I can reliably control, so that's where the rules are strictest. I also keep the heavy, risky work on my own machines, with their own off switch, so the cloud layer mostly sends missions and reads summaries.
On approval fatigue, I treat a card I approve without reading as a bug. If I approve the same kind of card three times without a second thought, it either becomes a narrow Always allow rule or the action should be redesigned so it doesn't need me. The goal is fewer, better cards.
On the reviewer, I follow the docs' own advice, which is also old security advice: least privilege first, explicit boundaries second, model review third. Dex Horthy's 12-factor agents puts it as a design rule: agents should "contact humans with tool calls." Asking me is a feature of the system, not an interruption of it.
And on the bigger worry, that I've built a second job maintaining the thing that was meant to save me time, I'll repeat what I wrote this morning. The setup only earns its place if Net Autonomy is positive. I can't prove that yet.
A super admin that can reach everything should be able to do almost nothing alone.
Net Autonomy is the only score that counts here
Here's how I'll score this layer. It's the same formula as everything else on this account, applied to the human side.
 
The third line of the supervision tax is the one I expect to hurt. Checking the phone "just in case" doesn't feel like work, so nobody counts it. It counts.
Here's the commitment, with dates.
This week. I start the weekly Net Autonomy log for the whole setup, including this layer: cards answered, drafts accepted and rejected, minutes spent supervising, and the number of times a bot reached me when it didn't need to.
Sunday 22 November. First numbers, in public, including the bad ones.
What would prove me wrong. If the supervision tax on this layer is bigger than the hours it returns for two weeks in a row, then the super admin is a hobby, not a system. I'll cut routines and bots until the number turns positive, and I'll say which ones I cut.
There's one more test, and it isn't a number. The foundation dossier ends its section on personal systems with a line I want to be judged by: "Its success is not continuous monitoring; its success is having more freedom to live well without staring at a dashboard." If this setup makes me look at my phone more, it has failed, whatever the log says.
The button that matters most
I started with a sentence about god mode. After living with it, I'd describe the setup differently.
Every machine I own is one sentence away. The bots can read almost anything, prepare almost anything, and dispatch missions to computers far more powerful than the phone in my hand. And the most important control in the whole system is a small card with two words on it.
Allow. Deny.
Everything else is plumbing. The value is that the plumbing runs while I'm training, cooking or out, and that it waits for me when it should.
If you run agents across more than one device, here's a question you can answer from your own week: how many approvals did you give last week without reading what you approved?
Count hours returned, not agents running.
 
Further reading worth saving
Grok Bot docs, "Overview." What a bot is, the shared cloud computer, routines and voice in one page.
Grok Bot docs, "Approvals, security, and privacy." Auto Review, approval cards, Ask first rules, local computer access, and the shared-computer boundary. The most useful page if you're setting up your own super admin.
Grok Bot docs, "Grok Bot for Mobile." What a bot can do with your phone's apps, the Action Button, and why the app has to be open.
Grok Bot docs, "Skills and routines." Schedules, event triggers, limits, cost, and "automate preparation before execution."
Grok Bot docs, "FAQ." Background work with the laptop closed, shared memory, and what requires approval.
Simon Willison, "The lethal trifecta for AI agents," June 2025. The best short explanation of why outward channels need the strictest rules.
Dex Horthy and HumanLayer, "12-factor agents." Small, focused agents, and contacting humans with tool calls.
Anthropic, "Building effective agents," December 2024. Simple, composable patterns, and when not to use agents at all.
Richard Cook, "How Complex Systems Fail." Read it before you give any one layer access to everything.
Gareth Altreality, "Decide Up, Work Down," 16 November 2026. The machine side of this setup: three layers, the 87% usage audit, and what broke.
Sources and status of each claim
Facts (public, with links)
Grok Bot capabilities: persistent cloud computer, background work with the laptop closed, shared computer across bots, registered computers with Execution on this computer (Ask every time by default), phone apps (calendar, contacts, location, alarms; reminders and Home on iPhone) only while the app is open, Action Button voice chat, Auto Review and approval cards, 20 Ask first and 20 Allow automatically rules of up to 1,000 characters, 30-minute expiry for background approvals, vault sign-ins and computer takeover, routines (50 per bot, five minutes apart minimum, 300 runs an hour across routines), and every quote attributed to "the docs": Grok Bot documentation at docs.x.ai, read 16 November 2026.
The lethal trifecta: Simon Willison, June 2025.
"Contact humans with tool calls": 12-factor agents, HumanLayer repository.
"Simple, composable patterns": Anthropic, December 2024.
Lived experience (my own setup, as of 16 November 2026)
Three registered Macs (two Mac Studios) and an iPhone; the connectors listed; the bot roster and their jobs; the five routines and their schedules; the X draft-then-"go" rule and the tweet and source reply that went out that way this morning; the request for this article dictated in French.
My own words to my bots: heavy work stays on the Macs, Grok Bot is the super admin that sends missions; and my earlier "shadow super admin" description, translated from French.
The usage audit (87% from three supervising bots; a 30-minute routine at about 336 runs a week and 4%): from "Decide Up, Work Down."
Method (my own frameworks)
Net Autonomy, the supervision tax, the Ask first rules, the routine template and the never-delegate list: my proposals, not validated standards. Quotes from the foundation dossier: Altreality: The Art of Living Free, foundation dossier, November 2026.
Interpretation
That permission, not reach, is where the value of a super admin sits.
That a roster of bots divides attention and cost, not trust.
That approving without reading is worse than not having approvals.
Hope and hypothesis
That this layer returns more hours than it costs. Unmeasured until the Net Autonomy log exists. First numbers promised for 22 November 2026.
The watcher's cost (about 8% of a week if it costs per run what the 30-minute routine did): an estimate, not a measurement.
That voice and phone actions return real time rather than making it easier to stay on call: untested.

现在很多人写代码已经离不开AI，但AI写得越快，人越看不过来。一个功能改十几个文件，自己从头读一遍要半小时，交给Claude Code去审，它又常常只挑几个文件看，报出来的行号对不上，同一段代码问两次结论还不一样。
这两天在GitHub上很火的阿里开源项目Open Code Review（命令叫ocr）就是专门解决这件事的。按官方说法，它原本是阿里集团内部的官方AI代码审查助手，内部用了两年，服务过数万名开发者，GitHub仓库今年5月创建。它的思路是：哪些文件要审、用什么规则审、评论落在哪一行，这些不能出错的环节交给写死的程序；真正读代码、找问题的部分才交给大模型。
几个核实过的数字（GitHub官方接口、npm官方接口和仓库README，东京时间2026年11月16日晚查询）：
星标52,585，Fork 4,224，当天GitHub Trending日榜新增691星
仓库创建于2026年5月18日，最新版v1.13.10发布于东京时间11月15日，11月5日到15日之间连发了5个版本
npm包@alibaba-group/open-code-review在11月9日到15日这一周下载175,982次
官方基准：从50个热门开源仓库挑出200个真实PR，覆盖10种语言，由80多位资深工程师标注出1,505个真实缺陷
协议为Apache-2.0，可以商用
这篇对照官方README、中文文档和命令行帮助整理。不需要模型的那部分功能（预览送审文件、查看和自定义审查规则），我在自己的Linux机器上装了v1.13.10，用一个演示项目实际跑了一遍，文中的命令输出都来自这次运行。

article.plain_text:
996,807 stars. That's what these ten repos add up to on GitHub today.
Most "best Claude skills" lists are a few months old, and in this space that's a long time. Anatomy didn't exist until October 8. Caveman and Taste Skill have been rebuilt since the spring. Every repo on this list was updated this month.
For each one: what it does, according to its own README, the install line, and when to reach for it.
Bookmark this. You'll want it the next time Claude hands you something that looks like everyone else's.
1. Superpowers · 304K ★
A full development method, not a prompt pack. Before writing code, the agent asks what you're actually trying to build, shows you the spec in short chunks, writes a plan with real red/green TDD, then runs the plan with subagents that review each other's work.
The README says it's not uncommon for the agent to work on its own for a couple of hours without drifting from the plan.
 
Use it when: you're building something real and Claude keeps jumping straight into code.
 
2. Frontend Design · Anthropic
Anthropic's own design skill, and the one Impeccable grew out of. Claude works as the design lead of a studio: it grounds the page in its subject, picks typefaces on purpose, and avoids the commonest tells of a generated page. The skill even lists them, from one italic word in the headline to a cream background with a terracotta accent.
 
Use it when: you need a landing page, dashboard or site that doesn't look generated.
 
3. Caveman · 115K ★
Makes your agent say less and read less, with the code kept exact. Version 4 has six parts: shorter answers, compressed logs and JSON before the model reads them, automatic model and effort choice, and reusable scripts.
Its README measures 63 tokens down to 20 for the same fix, 33.2% fewer input tokens per session, and 54% cheaper than Opus at xhigh at the same score.
 
Use it when: your bill or your context window is the problem, not the model.
 
4. Claude-Mem · 103K ★
Memory across sessions. It records what the agent does while it works, compresses it into summaries, and feeds the relevant parts back into the next session, so Claude stops rediscovering your project every morning.
 
Use it when: you work on the same codebase every day and keep re-explaining it.
 
5. Taste Skill · 102K ★
Gives coding agents taste for websites and app screens. It works from an art direction, finds real photographs in open archives (credited), and checks its own pages in a real browser instead of trusting the code.
 
Use it when: Frontend Design gets you a direction but the page still feels assembled.
 
6. Impeccable · 86K ★
A design vocabulary you share with the agent: 24 commands like polish, audit, critique, distill, bolder and quieter, plus 62 deterministic rules that catch the usual AI tells (Inter everywhere, cards inside cards, grey text on colour) without calling any model.
It started from Anthropic's Frontend Design and grew from there.
 
Use it when: you already have a UI and want it reviewed and tightened, not rebuilt.
 
7. Ruflo · 79K ★
An agent meta-harness for Claude Code and Codex: swarms of agents, coordinated workflows, a console to watch them, and mods that add routing and policy inside Claude Code. The README asks you to review the mods before installing, since they run with your account's permissions.
 
Use it when: one agent isn't enough and you want several working in parallel.
 
8. Anatomy · 20K ★
The most visual skill on this list. Ask how something works, and it invents a real machine whose working is the answer, then draws it as a detailed, shaded isometric figure with a live readout. A cache key becomes a pin-tumbler lock. It checks its own drawing by zooming in on every joint.
 
Use it when: you need to explain a technical idea in an article, docs or a landing page.
 
9. Remotion Agent Skills · 5.6K ★
The official skills from Remotion, the framework for making videos in React. They teach the agent compositions, animation timing, captions, audio and rendering, so "make me a promo video" ends in an MP4, not a broken timeline.
 
Use it when: you want video out of Claude, from code, with every frame under control.
 
10. Skill Creator · Anthropic
The skill that writes skills. It turns your own workflow into a skill Claude follows every time, then tests it with evals and benchmarks so you know it actually triggers and actually helps.
 
Use it when: you catch yourself typing the same instructions into Claude for the third time.
 
Where to start
If you install only three: Superpowers for how Claude works, one design skill (Frontend Design, Taste or Impeccable) for how its output looks, and Caveman for what it costs.
Star counts and install lines are from each repo as of this week. Check the README before installing anything that runs with your permissions.
Bookmark this so you don't lose it.
